Cover crops add root and shoot carbon inputs during otherwise fallow periods; the effect depends on cover-crop biomass production, which requires adequate off-season water.
In water-limited environments cover crops transpire stored soil water, which can leave less water for the following main crop.
More crop species in rotations or intercrops create more varied resources and microhabitats, increasing associated farmland biodiversity on average, though with high variability.
Diversified cropping provides flowering resources over a longer period, supporting pollinator communities.
Diversified rotations increase the quantity and diversity of residue and root inputs, supporting soil fertility services.
Legume intercrops in dryland systems add biologically fixed nitrogen and residue, improving soil organic carbon and fertility.
Intercropping raises within-field plant diversity, one form of crop diversification associated with higher farmland biodiversity.
Trees add vertical structure, perennial cover and habitat niches, increasing biodiversity relative to open cropland.
Tree biomass, litter fall and deep roots add carbon above and below ground, increasing soil carbon over decades.
Tree rows and woody patches add semi-natural habitat elements to simplified agricultural landscapes.

Flower strips and hedgerows provide nectar, pollen and nesting sites, increasing pollinator visitation to adjacent crops.
Uncropped field margins add permanent semi-natural habitat and connect habitat patches across the farm.

Reducing livestock grazing intensity lessens trampling and selective removal of plants, allowing plant and animal diversity to recover.

Reconnecting habitat fragments reduces edge effects and isolation, slowing species loss over time.
